messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have check some old post about setting multi-core running for INLA. Below is the code I used to run:

fit <- inla(f3,
                  family = "binomial",
                  lincomb = mylincomb,
                  data = inla.stack.data(mystack),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, openmp.strategy="huge"),
                  control.predictor = list(
                    A = inla.stack.A(mystack)),
                  control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"),
                  verbose=TRUE
)

I have a large data set of 181362 rows, with 11 covariates, a rw2 function and a spde.

I am running the script on a super computer with 72 cores and 400GB internal memory.

however, I dont see that I am runing on multi-cores, even after many hours so far. I am wondering whether there are part of the R-INLA procedure that are not able to run on multi-core (like an initialization step) that might take hours? Or if multi-core works, it should immediately start? (then in this case, my super computer does not allow multi-core)

Thanks

Chun Chen

messages.subject: Why adding a spatial spde gives extremely bad dic performance
messages.subject_clean: Why adding a spatial spde gives extremely bad dic performance
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running an analysis with and without a spatial spde model (I used a very coarse mesh with only 143 vertices). My data set have 181362 samples, I have 11 covariates and 1 year rw2 model in the model, as below:

### without spde
f3   <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + slope.std + aspect.std + gannet_dist.std +
    day_of_season.std + SOURCE_DBMWTL + sedimentDeep_sand + sedimentFine +
    sedimentFine_mud + sedimentMixed + sedimentSandy_mud + Dept1 +
    Dept2 + Dept3 + Dept4 + logopp + f(Year_std, model = "rw2")

M3 <- inla(f3,
                  family = "binomial",
                  lincomb = lcs.Dept,
                  data = inla.stack.data(Stack_Bern_gam_rw_year),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, openmp.strategy="huge"),
                  control.predictor = list(
                    A = inla.stack.A(Stack_Bern_gam_rw_year)),
                  verbose=TRUE
)

### with spde

f4  <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + slope.std + aspect.std + gannet_dist.std +
    day_of_season.std + SOURCE_DBMWTL + sedimentDeep_sand + sedimentFine +
    sedimentFine_mud + sedimentMixed + sedimentSandy_mud + Dept1 +
    Dept2 + Dept3 + Dept4 + logopp + f(Year_std, model = "rw2") +
    f(w, model = spde1)

M4 <- inla(f4,
                  family = "binomial",
                  lincomb = lcs.Dept,
                  data = inla.stack.data(Stack_Bern_gam_rw_year),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, openmp.strategy="huge"),
                  control.predictor = list(
                    A = inla.stack.A(Stack_Bern_gam_rw_year)),
                  verbose=TRUE
)

 When the model runs without the spatial spde, it gives a DIC of 80480. However, when I add the spatial spde, the DIC increased almost double to 168193. If I looked at the posterior mean of the spatial random field (see attachment), it is almost zero (as expected since my mesh is very coarse and my data might do not exist spatial correlation), except some boundary effect outside my sample area. It seems that with spde, the model becomes under-dispersed. I am wondering why adding a non-information (almost zero everywhere) spatial random field component could lead to such a bad fitting? Does anyone have any suggestions or comments?

Thanks very much

Regards,
Chun

Hi Chun,

Even though the posterior mean is small does not mean the random field is not used / uninformative. I am not surprised that the DIC can sometimes be worse.

I recommend trying the pc priors, and making the shrinkage stronger than what we usually use. See e.g.
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic108.html#5_the_model
Make the prior median for sigma small and the prior median for range big, this may improve the DIC of the spatial model.

Best,
Haakon

Hi,
You should be able to come up with a value that’s clearly “too large” for sigma; consider that your linear predictor is working in logit-space; not much variability is needed to make such models switch sharply between 0 and 1. You’re most likely interested in models that have smaller variability than that, so pick an upper quantile for sigma that would be unreasonable, and use a value as most as large as that when setting the parameters for the prior.

Finn

messages.subject: Large-scale posterior prediction
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using INLA to estimate large hierarchical and sometimes spatial models. These models have N > 500,000 nested in around 3000 hierarchical units. After a lot of small-scale tests, I have found that I am happy with the estimates generated with Gaussian approximation and EB integration. They are reasonable enough for my purposes, particular given the computational efficiency of this approach.

So, with that in mind, I am trying to find the most efficient way to use these models to generate a large number (e.g. > 800,000) of predictions.

Obviously, the canonical approach to prediction with INLA is to add the predictors and NA DV to the data matrix; however, this turns an already big computational problem into a really big one. My machine has 36 GB ram and I cannot fit this all in memory. So, to use this approach I've had to estimate the model several times and batch the predictions, which is hugely inefficient.

Write now, I'm working on functions that will let me easily sample from the posterior distribution (using inla.posterior.sample) and generate posterior predictions for arbitrary linear combinations of my predictors after fitting the model.

However, I am worried about the size of the sampled matrix (I haven't tried to run it on a full model, yet), since inla.posterior.sample seems to automatically sample for the linear predictor. For example, for a model with 600,000 observations, 1000 posterior samples for the linear predictor alone will be quite large.

Accordingly, I am wondering (1) if there is any way to suppress calculating the linear predictor in inla.posterior.sample().

However, more generally, I am wondering if there is a more efficient way to solve this problem. And, to, just to be clear, the problem is:

What is the most efficient way to generate posterior predictions for a large number of arbitrary combinations of predictors, given a large model with a large N.

And, again, I do not have sufficient RAM to estimate the model and all predictions simultaneously.

Also, I would greatly prefer to estimate the full posterior variance for the predictions, so the linear predictor alone isn't really sufficient.

Anyways, any advice on this would be extremely helpful, so thank you all in advance!

Best,
Joe

Hi,
I am trying to do prediction with samples from a large model. The model is expensive to fit, so getting predictions via refitting the model is not an option. The approach I take is that I use inla.posterior.sample to generate samples and plugin the samples coefficients to compute the linear predictor myself. As a sanity check, I looked if I can recover the "Predictor:XXXX" values in the samples. I am however unable to do this exactly, in particular the "Predictor:XXXX" values tend to be systematically slightly lower than what I compute myself. A short example using the binomial likelihood:
-----

library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)

logistic <- function(x) { 1 / (1 + exp(-x))}

n <- 10
data.test <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n,0,1)) %>% mutate(y = rbinom(n,size = 3, logistic(x * 1 + 5)))

ff <- inla(y ~ 1 + x , data = data.test, control.compute = list(config = TRUE), family = "binomial",Ntrials = 3)

st <- inla.posterior.sample(n= 1, ff)

expected_predictor <- st[[1]]$latent["(Intercept)",] + data.test$x * st[[1]]$latent["x",]

predictor_inla <- st[[1]]$latent[1:n]

data.frame(expected_predictor,predictor_inla) %>% mutate(difference = expected_predictor - predictor_inla)

st[[1]]$latent

-------

Do you have any ideas why this is the case? Is this expected behavior for some reason?

Thanks for any hints
Martin

Hi,

I think you’re on the right track with using inla.posterior.sample for this, since that both avoided some internal numerical issues besides the pure size aspect of doing the predictions inside inla().  I don’t know if sampling from the observation predictor can be avoided; possibly not, since it forms part of the internal model construction. For a purely Gaussian model it can be avoided in theory, but that would require writing special code for such models.  Hopefully Haavard will weigh in with more facts on that.

A workaround might be to not ask for all the samples at once, but rather ask inla.posterior.sample to produce only one realisation, and storing only the parts you need from that, and looping through until you have all the samples you want.
Needs some care with preallocating the data structure for storing the bits you want to keep to avoid unnecessary memory reallocations, but in principle this would let you produce an arbitrary amount of samples, provided that _one_ sample can be produced and then (partially) discarded.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thank you for this! I actually arrived at the same conclusion a little bit ago, so it is nice to have the approach confirmed.

I am also, it turns out, I am not entirely sure that I understand how to construct the posterior predictive distribution. If I use parameter samples drawn with inla.posterior.predict() to generate a distribution of predictions based on a linear combination of predictors, this provides an approximation of the posterior of the linear predictor, correct? From there, I need to incorporate error variance. In this thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/wIho_CZdcl4>, Håvard suggests this can be done as follows:

"I would use inla.posterior.sample() to generate (iid)
samples from the posterior and from this sample y_prd"

However, I am not totally sure what he means by "and from this sample y_prd". What I have done is:

1) Sample from posterior of linear predictor using inla.posterior.predict()
2) To predict for a new observation x, I use the posterior sample to calculate the linear prediction given x's values, which gives me a distribution of linear predictions.
3) For each sample i from the distribution of linear predictions, draw samples from a Gaussian distribution with mean equal to linear prediction i and SD equal to the estimated SD of the Gaussian observations.
3.1) Accordingly, if I have drawn 100 samples from the posterior of the linear predictor and I draw 100 samples for each of the linear predictor samples, I wind up with 100 x 100 predictions for the current new observation x. And, as I understand it, this is drawing from the posterior predictive distribution.
4) To estimate the SD of the posterior predictive distribution, take the SD of all draws from the posterior predictive distribution.

messages.subject: modeling different rates of success in a Bernoulli model
messages.subject_clean: modeling different rates of success in a Bernoulli model
messages.body_plain:
I would like to fit a Bernoulli model that separately models the probability of each event, because the true data has a right tail and I have an additional covariate that I believe helps me model that changing probability for each event, and thereby accommodate these outliers with an unusual probability of success that falls outside the range the binomial distribution would anticipate.

A logical option seems to be the beta-binomial model, with the binomial representing the Bernoulli likelihood and the beta distribution modeling the changing probability.

There may be a few issues.

First, beta-binomial models are often discussed in terms of finding overdispersion (variance exceeds mean), and I have seen it said that overdispersion cannot exist in a Bernoulli model, only an aggregated binomial.  I do not know if that “rule” affects what I am trying to do here or if it is even correct, but if so, what I am trying to do may not be useful if the beta binomial and the binomial likelihoods end up essentially collapsing to the same thing.

Second, assuming this is a reasonable approach, it is not clear to me how I signal to INLA through the formula interface which covariates I wish to assign to the beta likelihood versus the binomial likelihood, or if I even have the option of doing so separately.  INLA does seem to accommodate multiple likelihoods just fine in general, but I am having difficulty finding a worked example that would relate to what I am trying to do here.

For purposes of illustration, let’s let y be the output, a be the fixed effects for the binomial likelihood, z be a random effects vector for the binomial likelihood, and have c be the additional fixed effect I wish to fit solely (or also) to the beta distribution that drives changing probabilities of success.

Also, if there is another or better solution to this problem, in terms of fitting a different distribution or otherwise, I am all ears.  Many thanks.

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
If you want to predict a new observation from the fitted model, you can
do as follows:

   set.seed(1234)
   n = 100
   alpha = 1
   beta = 1
   s = 1
   z = rnorm(n)
   y = alpha + beta * z + rnorm(n, sd = s)
   r = inla(y ~ 1 + z,
           data = data.frame(y, z),

           control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
           family = "gaussian")

   x = inla.posterior.sample(10^4, r)

   znew = rnorm(1)
   fun = function(zz = NA) {
       return (Intercept + z * zz + rnorm(length(zz),
                                           sd = sqrt(1/theta[1])))
   }

   f1 = inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x, zz = znew)
   hist(f1[1, ], n = 100, prob = TRUE)
   m = alpha + beta * znew
   xx = seq(m-4*s, m+4*s, by = s/100)
   lines(xx, dnorm(xx, mean=m, sd = s), lwd=2)

which compares the posterior distribution from a new observation with
the one found from the fitted model.

Note that you need to know what 'theta' is, as its for the function
'fun', its only known as a vector.

inla.posterior.sample(), will by default, return samples of 'theta's in
the original parameterisation, meaning here, the precision. see the
help page.

you can also let 'znew' be a vector, for which you do this for several
new locations.

hope this helps.

H

PS: You can also process the output of posterior sample yourself, if
you rather want to, rather than using the '.fun' function.

Hi,
In order to predict at new locations, you need all the inputs of the model at those locations, and that includes the values of all the covariates you used to build the model.
If you don’t have the values of covariates, sometimes an option is to explicitly model the missing covariate values; for example, if a covariate is a slowly varying function of space, then you might build a spatial model for it, and include it in your overall model.
I believe there are such multivariate models among the spde examples on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>.

Finn

I have tried reinstalling both the stable and dev versions of INLA. I have also restarted R and not specified my Pardiso license, which I assumed would force reliance on the default computational approach.

I have also restarted my machine and immediately run the model on the simulated data. The model still crashed.

Any insight into what might be causing this and/or how to fix it would be hugely appreciated.

Thanks!

Best,
Joe

    f(year, model = "rw2", values = seq(1918,2001), hyper = hyper.prec) +

messages.subject_clean: What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running a R-inla model with a 2D spde involved. My samples are not evenly distributed, so I expect that the estimated spatial random field outside the sampling area are caused by the imposed matern correlation structure and mesh structure. Sometimes, I do obtain hot/cold spots in areas where no samples exits (not in the outside area of the defined mesh). In an extreme case, the posterior mean of the whole random spatial field only contains hot/cold spot outside sampling area while the sampling area is more or less constant.

Can some experts give some hints about what could cause these strange hot/cold spots? And how should we interpret and treat it?

Thanks very much!

Regards,
Chun

messages.body_plain:
Hi, easiest is probably to include the known mean as an offset in the model, either with offset() or by modifying the exposure, E.  In both cases, this requires doing that in a way that works with the LGCP likelihood setup. (Unless you don’t have an LGCP and just referred to that as an example).

I believe, but haven’t tested, that you can simply include the mean as an “effect” named e.g. myprocessmean in the inla.stack call just as you wold for a fixed effect covariate vector, associated with the same A matrix as the GP, and add
+offset(myprocessmean)
to the formula.
However, I’m not sure at what stage offset() is processed internally, so this might not work. If it fails, then I think the inlabru package should be able to do it (it parses the formula in a different way that allows more general R expressions).

Finn
